Audit, Risk and Improvement Committees in local government

Local Government

The Local Government Act 1993 requires every council to establish an Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee (ARIC). ARICs review council operations and provide independent advice to councils on matters including governance, risk management, financial management, compliance and strategic planning and reporting. 

Requirements for the composition, operation and oversight of ARICs are set out in the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021 and the Office of Local Government’s Guidelines for Risk Management and Internal Audit for Local Government in NSW. Councils have been required to establish an ARIC since 4 June 2022, with mandatory requirements relating to ARIC membership, risk management and internal audit taking effect from 1 July 2024. Councils must provide support to enable their ARIC to fulfil its responsibilities.
 

The audit will assess whether the Audit, Risk and Improvement Committees of selected councils are effectively fulfilling their responsibilities under section 428A of the Local Government Act 1993 and providing advice to councils to improve performance of their functions. The selected councils for this audit are Fairfield City Council, Goulburn Mulwaree Council and Narrabri Shire Council. The Office of Local Government, within the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure, is also included in the audit because of its role in providing relevant policy and guidance to the local government sector.

The audit will consider whether:

  • the ARIC reviews and provides advice to the council for the purpose of improving relevant council operations 
  • the council has effectively established and supports its ARIC to perform its required functions.

The period of review is from 2024-25 to present, reflecting when the Office of Local Government’s mandatory requirements came into effect. 
 

If you have experiences or views relevant to the audit scope, you can share them with the Audit Office. This can be done anonymously if you wish. Please note that contributions will close at 5pm, 4 December 2026.

Regulation of hazardous waste

Environment

Hazardous waste poses significant risks to public health, community safety and the environment if it is not managed, transported, treated and disposed of appropriately. 

The NSW Environment Protection Agency (EPA) has responsibility for regulating the use and disposal of waste that may be hazardous or potentially harmful to human health or the environment, such as hazardous chemicals, asbestos waste, construction and demolition waste. In New South Wales, hazardous waste is primarily regulated under the Protection of the Environment Operations Act 1997 and associated regulatory instruments.

This audit will assess whether the NSW EPA effectively regulates hazardous waste to deliver its legislative objective to reduce the risk of harm to human health and to the environment.

The audit will consider activities including: 

  • The EPA’s governance and oversight of the regulation of hazardous waste
  • The EPA's strategic framework to regulate hazardous waste
  • The EPA’s regulatory action to reduce risk of harm and respond to incidents relating to hazardous waste.

If you have experiences or views relevant to the audit scope, you can share them with the NSW Audit Office. This can be done anonymously if you wish. Please note that contributions will close at midnight on 6 December 2026.

You can contribute to this audit through the 'Contribute to this audit' button in the left-hand menu, the comment icon at the top right on mobile, or through this link.

If you would like to make a submission to the audit, please consider the following targeted questions:  

  1. What is your experience of the information available to understand your obligations for the management of hazardous waste? This may include information to support activities at any stage of the waste lifecycle. Please provide any examples to help us understand where the available information is sufficient, or where additional information may be of benefit. 
  2. What is your experience of the NSW EPA’s approach to conducting investigations on matters relevant to hazardous waste? Please provide any examples to help us understand what has worked well and what could be improved.

Health capital expenditure and infrastructure delivery

Health

NSW Health manages one of the largest capital programs in the state, with around $11.9 billion allocated over 4 years for health infrastructure. NSW Health capital spending is largely focused on building and redeveloping hospitals and health facilities. This audit will assess whether planning and delivery of major capital works is effective in meeting demand for health services in NSW. 

The auditees are:

  • Ministry of Health
  • Health Infrastructure

The audit will not assess:

  • the merits of government policy objectives
  • capital works delivered by NSW Health agencies other than Health Infrastructure
  • management and probity of tender processes

This audit will assess whether planning and delivery of major capital works is effective in meeting demand for health services in NSW.

The audit will assess the audit objective using the following criteria:

  1. Ministry of Health procedures for planning and prioritising investments in major health capital works are effective
  2. Health Infrastructure business cases are robust
  3. NSW Health project and program governance are effective in supporting the delivery of the health capital program and intended benefits

The audit will examine:

  • major NSW Health capital projects with an estimated total cost exceeding $100 million, managed by Health Infrastructure and subject to the Infrastructure Investor Assurance Framework
  • Ministry of Health procedures for planning and prioritising investments in major health capital works
  • development of business cases for major capital works led by Health Infrastructure
  • NSW Health project and program governance in supporting delivery of the health capital program and intended benefits.

Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund

Education

The NSW Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund (the Fund) was established under the Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund Act 2022 (the Act). The Fund aims to increase workforce participation, particularly for women, by making quality childcare more affordable and accessible. The NSW Government has committed up to $5 billion over ten years to invest in programs and initiatives that support these objectives. The Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund Board is responsible for developing strategic investment plans, developing programs, and administering financial assistance from the Fund. The Department of Education provides staff and services to support the Board's functions. The Act requires the Auditor-General to conduct a performance audit of the Fund at least once every three years.

This audit will assess whether the Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund is being administered effectively to achieve the objectives of the Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund Act 2022. 

The audit will address the following questions: 

  1. Have the Childcare and Economic Opportunity Fund Board and the Department of Education established governance, planning and program design arrangements that give effect to the objectives and requirements of the Act? 
  2. Are the Fund Board and the Department of Education administering and overseeing programs and financial assistance provided from the Fund to deliver the objectives of the Act?

Concord Hospital - request audit

Health

The NSW Minister for Health has requested that the Auditor-General conduct a performance audit of Concord Repatriation General Hospital. The audit follows concerns raised about governance, resourcing, workforce management and the hospital’s clinical and operational performance. The Audit Office recognises that some of these issues are sensitive and may be distressing for patients, staff and the broader community. The audit will consider these matters independently and objectively, with a focus on whether effective arrangements are in place to support the delivery of safe, efficient and effective health services at Concord Hospital.

This audit will assess whether the Ministry of Health and Sydney Local Health District have effective corporate governance, resource allocation, workforce governance, disciplinary practices and performance management arrangements to support the delivery of safe, efficient and effective services at Concord Hospital.

The audit will examine:

  • governance and accountability arrangements across the Ministry, Sydney LHD and Concord Hospital
  • the allocation of budget and workforce resources within Sydney LHD
  • workforce governance, including recruitment, promotion, complaint-handling and disciplinary processes, and the management of employee information
  • Concord Hospital's clinical, operational and workforce performance, and how this is monitored and managed.

Financial Management in Cultural Institutions

Industry

Effective financial management is critical in a fiscally constrained environment, where budget pressures and competing priorities increase the need to use public funds efficiently and sustainably. This audit will examine the effectiveness of financial management arrangements in selected cultural institutions (institutions) to fulfil their financial stewardship responsibilities and support long-term sustainability.

The audited entities are the Art Gallery of NSW, the Australian Museum and the Department of Creative Industries, Tourism, Hospitality and Sport. They were selected after considering risk, financial profile, sources of revenue, major projects, auditability and operating context. The audit may identify insights relevant to other entities in similar circumstances. Other institutions may be considered for future audits.

This audit will assess how effectively institutions manage and allocate their finances to achieve the prudent and efficient use of government resources.

The audit team will address the audit objective with the following criteria:

  1. The institutions have a financial management governance framework that is tailored to their operating context
  2. The institutions monitor and report on their financial position and risks using accurate and up-to-date data and systems
  3. The institutions make decisions to achieve public value, deliver planned benefits and the optimal use of resources.

Energy transition: coordinating enabling infrastructure and managing community impacts

Environment
Industry
Local Government
Planning
Premier and Cabinet
Transport
Whole of Government

The Electricity Infrastructure Roadmap is the NSW Government’s 20-year plan to transform the state’s electricity system into one that is affordable, clean and reliable.

This audit will assess whether relevant NSW Government agencies are effectively planning, coordinating and delivering the enabling infrastructure required for the Roadmap and managing associated impacts on local communities. The audit will focus on cross-government governance arrangements. This will be the first in a series of audits related to the energy transition.

For this audit, enabling infrastructure includes non-energy infrastructure, public services and supporting systems required to support the implementation of the Roadmap and Renewable Energy Zones and manage associated impacts on local communities. This may include roads and transport, housing and worker accommodation, water and wastewater infrastructure, and waste management.

The auditees are:

  • Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
  • Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure
  • Energy Corporation of NSW
  • Premier’s Department
  • Transport for NSW.

The audit will not assess:

  • the merits of renewable energy, Renewable Energy Zones or individual renewable energy projects
  • the boundaries of declared Renewable Energy Zones
  • the location of transmission corridors
  • infrastructure whose primary purpose is electricity generation, storage or transmission
  • community benefit payments that are not tied to specific infrastructure or service impacts.

This audit will assess whether NSW Government agencies are effectively planning and coordinating both the delivery of the enabling infrastructure needed to implement the Electricity Infrastructure Roadmap and the management of associated impacts on local communities.

The audit team will address the audit objective using the following criteria:

  1. Governance arrangements for coordinating enabling infrastructure and managing associated impacts on local communities enable the delivery of the Electricity Infrastructure Roadmap as a strategic priority of government.
  2. NSW Government agencies have prepared timely, evidence-based and deliverable plans for enabling infrastructure and associated community impact management, supported by costings, funding strategies and implementation pathways.
  3. NSW Government agencies are implementing agreed plans effectively and meeting their responsibilities to deliver enabling infrastructure and manage associated impacts on local communities.

You can provide information to the Audit Office if you have specific evidence relevant to the audit objective and criteria.

Submissions should relate directly to how NSW Government agencies have planned, coordinated or delivered enabling infrastructure, or managed associated impacts on local communities. They should identify the relevant agency, decision, plan, project or action and, where possible, include supporting documents, dates or other evidence.

The audit will not consider submissions about:

  • whether renewable energy or Renewable Energy Zones are desirable
  • the merits of individual renewable energy projects
  • the boundaries of Renewable Energy Zones
  • the location of transmission corridors
  • matters unrelated to the planning, coordination or delivery of enabling infrastructure and associated community impact management.

Submissions can be made anonymously. Please note that submissions close at 5 pm on 18 October 2026

Fisheries management and compliance

Industry

The objects of the Fisheries Management Act 1994 (the Act) are to conserve, develop and share the fishery resources of the state for the benefit of present and future generations. The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) is responsible for managing fisheries in NSW in line with the Act.

This audit will assess the effectiveness of DPIRD in regulating commercial fishing under the Act to contribute to the objects of conserving, developing, and sharing fishery resources in NSW.

The audit team will address the audit objective with the following criteria:

  1. DPIRD has arrangements and frameworks in place that enable it to effectively regulate commercial fishery requirements
  2. DPIRD effectively monitors commercial fishing operators and ensures their compliance with regulatory requirements.

Single Digital Patient Record

Health

The Single Digital Patient Record (SDPR) project aims to provide a secure, holistic and integrated view of the care a patient receives across the NSW Health system. It is designed to enable clinicians to access a patient’s medical information in real time from a single source. This audit will assess whether NSW Health effectively governed and implemented the initial stages phases of the SDPR program to deliver its intended outcomes and inform subsequent rollout phases.

This audit will assess whether NSW Health effectively governed and implemented the initial phases of the Single Digital Patient Record (SDPR) program to deliver intended outcomes and inform subsequent rollout phases.

We will address the audit objective by answering the following questions:

  1. Has NSW Health established and maintained effective governance of the SDPR program?
  2. Has the Single Digital Patient Record Implementation Authority (SDPRIA) effectively implemented the initial phases of the SDPR program?

If you have experiences or views relevant to the audit, you can share them with the Audit Office. This can be done anonymously if you wish. Please note that contributions will close at 6pm, Friday 4 December 2026.

You can give feedback to this audit either through the 'Contribute to this audit' button in the left hand menu (comment icon on top right for mobile) or through this link 

We may use your contribution to identify key themes, risks or issues which may then be further investigated during the audit. In some instances, we may use extracts of what you tell us in our audit report as examples of feedback provided where appropriate. If we use extracts of a contribution, we will not identify the source in the report.

We will not share feedback provided to us with any other organisation or person outside of the Audit Office, and we will not publish feedback (including formal submissions) in our reports or on our website.

  • Performance audits focus on assessing whether public money is spent efficiently, effectively, economically and in compliance with the law. The Auditor-General is not permitted to question the merits of government policy objectives (see subsection 27B(6) of the Government Sector Audit Act).
